transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-07-30
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~75 minutes
Attendees: Miguel Ortiz (Redwood AE), Sana Kapoor (Redwood SE), Anita Rao (Keelbridge VP Eng), Marcus Lee (Keelbridge SRE), Tobias Nguyen (Security), Priya Sharma (Platform)

Summary:
Quick network + runtime deep dive to diagnose p95/p99 tail issues seen when Keelbridge runs inference through PrivateLink to Redwood Private. Main threads: NAT hairpin latency spikes, DNS resolver timeouts, KV cache affinity causing cold miss penalties, and batching/window tuning with quantized models.

Topics:
- PrivateLink interface endpoints and cross-account ENI behavior
- NAT Gateway vs Shared NAT vs egress proxy (hairpin cases)
- DNS resolver timeouts and conditional forwarding to on-prem resolvers
- KV cache affinity and stickiness for latency-sensitive routes
- Batching window vs continuous batching tradeoffs for p99
- Int8 quantization tail behavior and kernel selection fallbacks

Action items (brief): see action_items metadata above

Transcript body:
00:00 Miguel: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, um, we'll kick off. I see the main symptom is spikes in p95/p99 during certain traffic patterns, is that right Anita?
00:12 Anita: Yeah, correct. We're seeing occasional 200-600ms spikes on top of a 60-80ms baseline for generation calls. It mostly happens during bursts when multiple clients concurrently request long sequences.
00:25 Sana: And are those routed through your PrivateLink interface endpoints or do you have an egress path via a NAT GW?
00:33 Marcus: Primary path is PrivateLink to Redwood's VPC endpoint in our account, but we also have an egress path for some workflows that still go through our NAT to the internet for hosted dominoes — sorry, hosted endpoints — bad word, basically to external APIs. There are a couple of cross-account routes.
00:48 Miguel: Got it. Two quick clarifications: one, when you say PrivateLink are you using interface endpoints in the same account or cross-account? Two, any intermediate proxies or sidecars performing TLS termination?
01:00 Marcus: Cross-account, interface endpoints in our account with VPC endpoint service on Redwood side. We do have a sidecar in front of the app that does some auth and mTLS offload, but it shouldn't touch the Redwood connection directly.
01:14 Tobias: We do terminate TLS at the proxy for inbound, but connections to external services are typically passthrough. Still, there might be SNI-based routing in the proxy.
01:23 Sana: OK that SNI bit is important — SNI mismatches can lead to connection churn if your proxy reuses different upstream connections. Also, interface endpoints create ENIs in subnets; if those ENIs get exhausted you can see purple — so-called connection queuing — which looks like latency spikes.
01:40 Anita: We saw ENI counts spike, yeah. At one point the account hit ENI quotas on two subnets. We increased quotas but I don't think that was the whole story.
01:48 Miguel: Right. Two likely culprits then: ENI exhaustion/connection pooling and NAT hairpin behavior. Hairpinning is when requests go out and back into the same VPC causing weird pathing and double-NAT. That can add jitter, especially with large packets if MTU is mismatched.
02:05 Marcus: MTU — we've seen fragmentation on the path to Redwood in a few tests. When we run longer sequences we see more fragmentation, and at high concurrency this aligns with spikes.
02:15 Sana: Are you on AWS? Fragmentation with PrivateLink + Transit Gateway + NAT can happen. If you have a transit gateway in front, sometimes the MTU is reduced to 1436 and clients with 1500 will fragment.
02:26 Priya: We're on AWS, yes TGW in our core. We have mixed subnets: some private with NAT GW, some with local egress via transit.
02:34 Miguel: Important fix: enable Path MTU discovery end-to-end and avoid manual MTU clamping in your proxies. Also, ensure ENI warmup: keep long-lived HTTP/2 or HTTP/1.1 keep-alives so TCP openings are amortized.
02:48 Marcus: We do keepalives but the sidecar sometimes closes idle connections aggressively after 30s; maybe that's killing pooling.
02:54 Sana: That explains it — connection churn triggers new TLS handshakes and SNI negotiation, adding 30-200ms per request depending on CPU. For the inference path, our recommended pattern is: increase upstream keepalive to 5m, use connection pooling, and avoid per-request TLS renegotiation.
03:12 Miguel: Next, KV cache behavior: you mentioned before that cold misses cause large penalties?
03:17 Anita: Yes, when the KV cache isn't locally hit we see an extra 120ms. With long-running chats that store prefix KV, it's pretty bad.
03:25 Sana: Two knobs: affinity (stick the same user's affinity to the same runtime node to keep KV hot) and prefix caching at the app layer. Affinity reduces cross-node KV misses but can hurt load distribution during spikes.
03:38 Tobias: For security reasons we try not to keep user data pinned long-lived on a single GPU host; we do ephemeral affinity for the duration of a session only. Is ephemeral affinity supported?
03:47 Miguel: Yes, Redwood Private supports session-level KV affinity via sticky routing token — it's configurable in rollout policies. You can set a TTL for affinity; when TTL expires the routing will rebalance. Also, there's per-route cache priming we can suggest.
04:01 Marcus: How does batching interact? If affinity pins to a node, does that reduce effective batching because requests go to the same worker?
04:09 Sana: It can change the batching mix. Continuous batching is worker-local — it batches requests coming to that worker. If affinity clusters too strongly to a single worker that can actually increase effective batch size which may be good for throughput but could increase tail due to serialization and longer batch windows. We typically tune the batching window and max batch size per model and per workload.
04:28 Miguel: For Keelbridge use case, we think p95 spikes are a mix: KV cold misses (120ms), TLS connection churn (30-200ms), and MTU/fragmentation (variable). Quantization tail behavior can add some jitter too — when we fall back from int8 fast kernels to fallback paths for certain operators you'll see another 20-80ms.
04:48 Priya: That fallback sounds scary — why would the runtime fallback?
04:52 Sana: If a particular operator pattern isn't covered by the optimized kernel for int8 or if input shapes are edge-case we sometimes route to a slower kernel path. We log those fallbacks but if logging isn't surfaced you won't notice. We can add telemetry on kernel selection and quantization deoptimization counts.
05:07 Miguel: We should instrument kernel fallback rates alongside KV miss rates and ENI churn. If they correlate with the spikes that's a smoking gun.
05:15 Anita: Good plan. For the PrivateLink path, we also saw intermittent DNS timeouts when our resolver chain hit our on-prem forwarders. That added 150-300ms on cold queries.
05:26 Sana: DNS matters more than people think. If your app does an initial hostname lookup per request (instead of keeping the connection open), you get DNS jitter. Recommend resolving once and reusing or reducing TTL lookups. For interface endpoints, use the AWS-provided resolver in the subnet and ensure conditional forwarding is low-latency.
05:42 Marcus: We do run DNS over TLS in the cluster, which adds CPU and occasionally delays.
05:47 Tobias: The TLS to resolver was instituted for PII controls; we can maybe whitelist Redwood IPs to avoid extra hops.
05:54 Miguel: Fine short-term mitigation: a dedicated resolver in the same AZ as the callers pointed at Redwood's IP; long-term: add pinned connections and increase keepalive and DNS caching.
06:05 Sana: Also ensure the PrivateLink endpoint's security group allows high connection counts and ephemeral ports. Sometimes default SG rules throttle new conn bursts.
06:15 Marcus: On quotas, we did bump ENI quotas but didn't increase ephemeral port ranges on our firewall. That might be the limit.
06:22 Miguel: Right, ephemeral port exhaustion can masquerade as backpressure. Add monitoring on ephemeral port usage.
06:30 Anita: Can Redwood provide a checklist for subnet sizing, ENI counts, and PrivateLink best practices?
06:35 Miguel: Yes — we'll send a checklist. It includes: subnets per AZ, ENI headroom, endpoint service scaling, MTU guidance, keepalive settings, DNS resolver placement, and recommended affinity TTL values.
06:47 Sana: On KV cache affinity experiments: propose A/B where half traffic uses affinity TTL=5m and half uses no affinity, measure p50/p95/p99 and token cost. Also test packing small requests to increase batch efficiency.
06:58 Marcus: For packing, some of our clients send many small requests; do you recommend client-side batching or let Redwood batch on server?
07:06 Sana: Both. Client-side packing reduces request/response overhead. Server-side continuous batching helps for unpredictable arrival. For latency-sensitive flows, small server-side batch windows (5-15ms) plus client pack when possible is a good combo.
07:18 Miguel: We should also consider per-model quantization profiles. For the large generation models you might run int8; for small models maybe int4 is fine. Quantization changes latency and kernel selection, so include that in the interim benchmark.
07:30 Priya: Any security concerns with affinity? If a session sticks to a node, does that change audit or encryption-handling?
07:36 Tobias: From security perspective we want session-based ephemeral keys and audit logs for any KV use.
07:41 Miguel: Redwood Private supports per-session encryption and audit logs; we can scope key access policies in KMS. We'll include a short security appendix.
07:50 Anita: Okay, recap: run lab for MTU and NAT hairpin tests, give checklist, and instrumentation plan.
07:55 Miguel: Yup. We'll follow up with dates. Anything else?
08:00 Marcus: Quick question — for interface endpoints, do you recommend per-AZ endpoints or a shared endpoint per region?
08:06 Sana: Per-AZ is best for low latency and to avoid cross-AZ egress; use one endpoint per AZ with route table controls. Shared per-region endpoints can introduce cross-AZ hops.
08:18 Miguel: We'll also provide example iptables rules and an eBPF snippet to count ephemeral ports and active connections per ENI.
08:26 Anita: Thanks all.
08:29 Miguel: Thanks — action items in the notes. We'll send materials and propose the lab window.
08:34 Meeting end.

Notes on transcription quality: speakers overlapped twice, some product names transcribed incorrectly (e.g., "dominoes" -> "endpoints"). Timestamp markers are approximate.
